title: The global digital divide
subtitle: A third of humanity offline
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: 2.7 billion people still do not have access to the Internet. In an increasingly digital world, this lack of connection becomes a new form of exclusion.

hero.hook: Kenya invented payment by telephone ten years before Europe, due to a lack of bank branches.

blocks.text: While developed societies are experiencing a revolution driven by artificial intelligence, a brutal reality persists: **2.7 billion people**, or around a third of humanity, still do not have access to the Internet.

This **digital divide** is not just a technical delay: it has become a real barrier, which keeps millions of people away from education, health and the global economy. Here's why it persists, and how some countries are trying to fill it.

By 2024, around 5.4 billion people will be connected to the Internet worldwide, but progress is stagnating in the poorest regions. Europe and North America exceed 90% connection, while sub-Saharan Africa remains at only 37%.

This exclusion is due to several causes. First, the lack of infrastructure: installing optical fiber in certain isolated regions is considered too costly by operators. Then, the price: in some countries, a simple entry-level  represents several months' salary. Finally, the language barrier (around 70% of web content is in English) and the lack of digital training limit use even when a connection exists. [[smartphone]]

sections.title: When lack of infrastructure forces innovation

blocks.text: This divide acts as a multiplier of inequalities. In a world where remote working, e-commerce and online education (the ) are becoming the norm, not being connected means becoming invisible to the global economy. [[MOOC]]

blocks.caption: In many rural areas, the mobile phone remains the only point of access to the Internet.

blocks.text: Kenya illustrates another path: due to a lack of sufficient bank branches, the country massively adopted a simple SMS payment system in 2007, , ahead of Europe by ten years. This system has allowed millions of people without bank accounts to make secure transactions with a simple phone. [[Kenyan M-Pesa]]
Kenya has dubbed this strategy technological leapfrogging: rather than installing expensive and outdated infrastructure, the country moved directly to a more modern and cheaper solution.

To connect the most isolated villages, new players are banking on space. The  project sends thousands of satellites into low orbit, allowing rapid connection even in deserts or high mountains, without having to lay a single cable. [[Starlink (SpaceX)]]

But the cost of the subscription and equipment remains aligned with Western standards, which makes these solutions inaccessible to the poorest rural populations without external assistance. Resolving the digital divide cannot therefore be achieved through technology alone: ​​it also requires political will to make the Internet something accessible to all.

The rapid rise of artificial intelligence threatens to further widen this divide. It requires immense computing and data power, resources concentrated in the hands of a few countries and companies. Disconnected populations then risk becoming dependent on tools designed without taking into account their culture or language.

The skills gap between connected and unconnected students could also widen very quickly. The challenge for the coming years will therefore no longer be just to provide a connection, but to guarantee fair access to the creation of digital value, by combining lower costs, local content and training.

2.7 billion people remain excluded from the Internet today, a divide that risks worsening with artificial intelligence. Reducing this gap requires transforming connectivity into a real good accessible to all, and not just a product to sell.
